ASGE Guideline on Management of Esophageal and Gastric Varices in Patients with Cirrhosis
  • Source: Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, Vol. ■, No. ■ : 2026
  • Topic: Management of esophageal and gastric varices in patients with cirrhosis
  • Author(s): ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Marya NB, Cosgrove N, Thiruvengadam NR, et al.)
Background on Varices in Cirrhosis
  • ~40% of patients with cACLD will develop varices annually
  • 5%-15% of cACLD patients with varices will decompensate and experience variceal bleeding
  • Variceal bleeding is a serious cause of morbidity and mortality
  • Endoscopy plays important role in screening and management
Key Definitions Used in This Guideline
  • cACLD: significant hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis without current/prior clinical decompensation
  • Decompensated cirrhosis: development of overt ascites, variceal hemorrhage, or overt hepatic encephalopathy
  • CSPH: hepatic venous pressure gradient ≥10 mm Hg → increased risk of decompensation and death
  • High-risk esophageal varices: moderate/large-size or any size with high-risk bleeding stigmata (red wale signs, cherry-red spots)
  • High-risk gastric varices: actively bleeding, previously bled, high-risk stigmata, or >10 mm in size
  • Emergent endoscopy: within 12 hours of presentation
  • Urgent endoscopy: within 24 hours of presentation
  • PEI: endotracheal intubation performed only for airway protection before upper endoscopy
Screening for Varices in cACLD
Baveno VI Criteria for High-Risk Varices
  • Recommendation: ASGE suggests use of Baveno VI criteria to screen for high-risk varices
  • Conditional recommendation / Low certainty evidence
Baveno VI Criteria Application
  • Patients with liver stiffness <20 kPa AND platelets >150,000/μL → screening endoscopy may be avoided
  • Assessment should repeat annually; endoscopy performed when liver stiffness ≥20 kPa or platelets ≤150,000/μL
Baveno VI Performance
  • Sensitivity: 97% (95% CI, 0.95–0.98) for detecting high-risk varices
  • Specificity: 32% (95% CI, 0.26–0.39) for detecting high-risk varices
  • Based on meta-analysis of 30 studies (mostly retrospective)
Baveno VI Limitations and Exclusions
  • Should NOT be applied to patients with:
  • Decompensated cirrhosis (especially significant ascites or prior variceal bleeding)
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Prior splenectomy
  • Not validated in pediatric/adolescent populations → these patients should undergo endoscopic surveillance
Transient Elastography Considerations
  • Most common transducer: FibroScan (Echosens, Paris)
  • Limited diagnostic accuracy for patients with high BMI
  • Performs well for BMI <40 kg/m²
  • For BMI >40 kg/m² → consider MR elastography (though Baveno VI not validated with MR)
  • ASGE cannot provide additional recommendations for higher BMI patients
Baveno VII Criteria (Updated)
  • Published recently with more nuanced recommendations
  • Uses combinations of liver stiffness and platelet measurements
  • Baveno VII criteria can result in fewer endoscopies vs Baveno VI
  • Prospective study showed lower "miss rate" of higher risk varices with Baveno VI vs VII
  • Panel limited recommendation to Baveno VI due to lack of robust data for Baveno VII
Sustainability
  • Use of noninvasive approaches (Baveno VI) may decrease unnecessary endoscopy and procedural burden
Management of cACLD with CSPH
Initial Endoscopic vs Pharmacologic Approach
  • Recommendation: ASGE suggests prescribing carvedilol with surveillance endoscopies at least every 12 months
  • Conditional recommendation / Low quality of evidence
Evidence for Carvedilol vs VBL
  • Meta-analysis by Sharma et al (12 RCTs, >800 patients):
  • All-cause mortality: no difference between NSBB or VBL (OR, 1.35; 95% CI, 0.98–1.86)
  • VBL associated with ↓ odds of variceal bleeding vs NSBB (OR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.35–0.78)
  • Subanalysis of 2 RCTs comparing carvedilol vs VBL:
  • All-cause mortality: no difference (OR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.48–1.54)
  • Variceal bleeding: no difference (OR, 1.50; 95% CI, 0.49–4.60)
Newer RCTs Showing Mortality Benefit
  • Meta-analysis by Villanueva et al (4 RCTs evaluating carvedilol and VBL):
  • Decompensation prevention: carvedilol ↓ risk vs placebo/endoscopy (OR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.29–0.89)
  • All-cause mortality: carvedilol ↓ risk vs placebo/endoscopy (subdistribution HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.19–0.90)
  • Benefits appeared driven by 2 newer RCTs
  • In newer RCTs: 16%–20% of patients receiving carvedilol developed high-risk varices and required band ligation
Carvedilol Dosing
  • Start: 3.125 mg twice daily or 6.25 mg daily
  • Titrate upward as allowed by blood pressure
  • Keep SBP >90 mm Hg and mean arterial pressure >65 mm Hg
  • Maximum dose: 12.5 mg per day (can increase further for nonhepatic reasons)
  • Unlike other beta-blockers (titrated to HR 55–60 bpm), carvedilol titrated by blood pressure
Contraindications to NSBB/Carvedilol
  • Hypotension (SBP <90 mm Hg)
  • Severe asthma or severe COPD
  • Acute kidney injury
  • Bradycardia (resting HR <55 bpm)
  • Patients unable to tolerate side effects (dizziness, fatigue)
Alternative When NSBB Not Tolerated
  • If carvedilol cannot be prescribed → upper endoscopy at least every 12 months, with VBL as needed
Antibiotic Therapy for Upper GI Bleeding in Cirrhosis
Prophylactic Antibiotics
  • Recommendation: ASGE suggests antibiotics be prescribed to prevent bacterial infection
  • Conditional recommendation / Very low certainty of evidence
Evidence for Antibiotic Prophylaxis
  • Meta-analysis (15 RCTs, 1322 patients) from 1995–2023:
  • All-cause mortality: no significant difference (RD, 2.1%; 95% CI, –1.9 to 6.6)
  • Probability of noninferiority: 89.8%
  • Subanalysis post-2004 RCTs: probability of noninferiority 98.9%
  • Subanalysis pre-2004 RCTs: probability of noninferiority 72.4%
  • Early recurrent bleeding: no significant difference (RD, 4.0%; 95% CI, –4.2 to 12.3)
  • Bacterial infections: ↓ with prophylactic antibiotics (RD, 18.8%; 95% CI, 8.6–29.4)
Quality of Evidence Concerns
  • Several RCTs unblinded
  • Some studies did not exclude patients with active infections at randomization
  • Inadequate a priori sample size calculations and power analyses
  • None of included studies reported data on patients lost to follow-up
Important Considerations
  • Most recent RCT (2023) demonstrated no mortality benefit for antibiotic prophylaxis
  • More recently, patients receiving third-generation cephalosporins → ↑ concern for C difficile infection
  • Practitioners should weigh benefit vs risk of antibiotic-associated infections
Future Directions
  • Additional RCTs required to clarify role of antibiotic prophylaxis in this population
Duration of Vasoactive Pharmacotherapy
Short vs Long Course
  • Recommendation: ASGE suggests short-term administration (2–3 days) of vasoactive medications is sufficient
  • Conditional recommendation / Low certainty of evidence
Evidence for Short-Duration Therapy
  • Meta-analysis of 14 RCTs comparing:
  • Short-term: total duration <3 days after presentation
  • Long-term: total duration 3–5 days after presentation
  • Outcomes at 5-day (early) and 6-week (delayed) time points:
  • Early recurrent bleeding: no difference (RR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.37–1.65)
  • Delayed recurrent bleeding: no difference (RR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.46–1.30)
  • Mortality from recurrent bleeding: no difference (RR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.26–2.13)
  • Overall mortality: no difference (RR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.62–1.71)
  • Length of hospital stay: shorter with short-term therapy (MD, –1.12 days; 95% CI, –1.42 to –0.30)
Timing of Vasoactive Medications
  • Start as soon as feasible once variceal bleeding suspected
  • May be stopped after appropriate duration of therapy completed
Special Consideration for Sclerotherapy
  • Subgroup analysis: shorter vasoactive therapy with sclerotherapy → more recurrent bleeding and greater mortality in extended period
  • Sclerotherapy may cause acute rise in portal pressure lasting up to 5 days
  • Authors encourage longer vasoactive therapy duration of 5 days for patients undergoing sclerotherapy
Timing of Endoscopy in Suspected Variceal Hemorrhage
Emergent vs Urgent Endoscopy
  • Recommendation: ASGE suggests endoscopy within 24 hours for suspected variceal bleeding
  • Additional decision-making based on patient's clinical presentation (resuscitation status, hemodynamic status, active bleeding)
  • Conditional recommendation / Very low certainty of evidence
Evidence for Timing
  • Meta-analysis of 9 observational studies (6 evaluated specifically):
  • Endoscopy within 12 hours vs not:
  • Overall mortality: no significant difference (OR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.38–1.38)
  • Recurrent bleeding: no difference (OR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.55–1.95)
  • Length of hospital stay: no difference (MD, –0.28 days; 95% CI, –1.26 to 0.70)
  • Hemostasis: no difference (OR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.27–1.15)
  • One study evaluated endoscopy within 24 hours vs after:
  • Fewer deaths with <24 hours, but not statistically significant (OR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.02–1.36)
ASGE Recommendation Change
  • Previous ASGE guidance: within 12 hours
  • Current guideline: within 24 hours acceptable
Preprocedure Considerations
  • Maintain adequate vascular access (at least 2 large-bore IV catheters)
  • Fluid resuscitation with colloid or crystalloid
  • Restrictive transfusion target: hemoglobin 7–8 g/dL (absence of ischemic comorbidities, ongoing bleeding, hemodynamic instability)
  • Overtransfusion may worsen portal hypertension-related bleeding
  • Platelet counts >50 × 10⁹/L and fibrinogen >120 mg/dL previously targeted (no longer routinely recommended)
  • Elevated PT/INR not reflective of coagulative state in cirrhosis patients not on antithrombotic agents
  • Thromboelastography provides more accurate assessment of coagulopathy
Prophylactic Endotracheal Intubation (PEI)
PEI in Suspected Variceal Hemorrhage
  • Recommendation: ASGE suggests against routine PEI for all patients with suspected variceal bleeding
  • Additional decision-making based on clinical presentation (resuscitation status, mental status, hemodynamic status, active bleeding)
  • Conditional recommendation / Very low certainty of evidence
Evidence Against PEI
  • Meta-analysis of 7 studies comparing PEI vs no PEI before endoscopy:
  • For all upper GI bleeding patients:
  • Mortality: similar (OR, 1.92; 95% CI, 0.71–5.23)
  • Aspiration: ↑ with PEI (OR, 3.85; 95% CI, 1.46–10.15)
  • Hospital stay: longer with PEI (MD, 0.86 days; 95% CI, 0.13–1.59)
  • For variceal hemorrhage specifically (2 observational studies):
  • Mortality: significantly higher with PEI (OR, 3.47; 95% CI, 1.24–9.74)
  • Aspiration: similar (OR, 4.60; 95% CI, 0.53–39.91)
  • Hospital stay: similar (MD, 0.22 days; 95% CI, –0.08 to 0.53)
Important Considerations for PEI
  • This guideline specifically discusses PEI for endoscopic procedures only
  • Does not apply to other indications: acute respiratory failure, inability to protect airway, significantly impaired mental status, massive ongoing hematemesis
  • Patients unable to protect airway due to emesis or mental status changes require endotracheal intubation
  • Discuss potential need for intubation with anesthesia and critical care teams on case-by-case basis
  • Studies primarily evaluated adult populations → recommendations may not apply to pediatric/adolescent patients
Refractory Bleeding Esophageal Varices
Balloon Tamponade vs Esophageal Stents
  • Recommendation: ASGE suggests either fully covered esophageal stents OR balloon tamponade as bridge to definitive therapy (eg, TIPS)
  • Based on institutional expertise
  • Conditional recommendation / Very low certainty of evidence
Evidence for Esophageal Stents
  • Single RCT across 9 Spanish hospitals comparing:
  • Esophageal balloon tamponade (n=15)
  • Covered esophageal stent placement (n=13)
  • Used SX-ELLA-CS stent (currently unavailable in US):
  • Fully covered nitinol stent
  • 25-mm body diameter, 30-mm flare diameter, 135-mm length
  • Approved for placement up to 7 days
  • Outcomes in refractory/massive bleeding:
  • Immediate hemostasis: stent 66% vs balloon 20% (P=.025)
  • Recurrent bleeding at 15 days: stent 15% vs balloon 53% (P=.037)
  • Device-related serious adverse events: stent 8% vs balloon 40% (P=.049)
  • 6-week mortality: stent 46% vs balloon 60% (P=.46)
Stent Availability and Selection
  • SX-ELLA stent not available in US → limits generalizability
  • Other fully covered metal stents available in US (some deployable through endoscope)
  • Only fully covered self-expandable metal stents should be used
  • Choose largest available stent diameter to facilitate mechanical varix compression
  • Place stents so majority (at least two-thirds) is within esophagus
Stent Contraindications and Complications
  • Do not place in setting of known/suspected gastric variceal bleeding
  • Only as bridge to more definitive therapy → can be removed endoscopically
  • Ongoing bleeding despite stent placement: manage with balloon tamponade and/or emergent TIPS
Institutional Expertise Considerations
  • Stent placement often requires advanced endoscopy training
  • Many physicians managing esophageal varices do not have advanced training
  • Despite improved outcomes vs balloon tamponade, panel suggests either technique can be considered
Management of High-Risk Gastric Varices
Approach Overview
  • More complex than esophageal varices → requires multidisciplinary approach
  • Consider: underlying disease, vascular anatomy, presence of shunts/thrombosis, comorbidities
Initial Management in Acute Bleeding
  • Focus on resuscitation and timely hemostasis
  • Dictated by local resources and available expertise
  • Hemostatic techniques:
  • Endoscopic intervention
  • Balloon tamponade
  • Radiologic intervention (TIPS, RTO)
Stable Patients with High-Risk Gastric Varices
  • Perform 3-phase CT scan before intervention
  • Assess for large splenorenal shunt (↑ risk of systemic embolization)
  • Consider transthoracic echocardiogram with bubble agitation study
  • Evaluate for patent foramen ovale
Multidisciplinary Discussion
  • Discuss findings with interventional radiologists, hepatologists, transplant surgeons
  • Essential for treatment planning
Ongoing Management After Endoscopic Therapy
  • Patients warrant ongoing endoscopic surveillance
  • Continue NSBB use
  • Consider more definitive radiologic management as appropriate
Endoscopic Therapy for High-Risk Gastric Varices
EUS-Guided vs Direct Endoscopic Injection
  • Best Practice Advice: ASGE suggests EUS-guided injection (EUS-I) over direct endoscopic injection (DEI) for high-risk gastric varices
  • When EUS-I performed → suggest EUS-CYA plus coils vs EUS-CYA alone, when feasible
  • If EUS-guided expertise unavailable → DEI can be performed
  • Conditional recommendation / Very low certainty of evidence
Gastric Variceal Classification (Sarin Classification)
  • GOV1: varices on lesser curvature extending from GE junction
  • Band ligation is effective and accepted management
  • IGV1/GOV2 (cardiofundal gastric varices):
  • Band ligation NOT effective due to vascular depth and anatomy
  • Management centers on thrombotic agent injection (eg, CYA) into high-risk varix or feeder vessel
Evidence for EUS-I vs DEI
  • Systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies:
  • >800 patients underwent EUS treatment
  • >3400 patients underwent DEI for high-risk gastric varices
  • Most studies retrospective, many single-arm
Outcomes Comparison (EUS-I vs DEI)
Outcome EUS-I DEI
Technical success 94% (95% CI, 90–96%) 91% (95% CI, 83–96%)
Obliteration of gastric varices 84% vs 63% (P=.02) —
Recurrence of gastric varices 9% vs 18% (P=.06) —
Early recurrent bleeding 7% vs 5% Similar
Late recurrent bleeding 12% vs 17% Similar
Subgroup Analysis: EUS-CYA + Coils vs DEI
  • Patients receiving EUS-CYA + coils had:
  • Higher obliteration rates: 86% vs 63% (P=.02)
  • Lower recurrence rates: 5% vs 18% (P=.01)
Recent RCTs Supporting EUS-I
  • Single-center RCT of 43 patients (primary prophylaxis):
  • EUS-CYA into perforator (feeder) vessel vs DEI
  • At 3 months: variceal obliteration 77.2% vs 38.1% (P=.014)
  • Required less CYA: 1 mL vs 2 mL (P=.027)
  • RCT of 96 patients comparing EUS-CYA vs DEI for IGV1:
  • Lower recurrent bleeding, overall recurrence, and cumulative nonbleeding at up to 24 months (P<.05)
  • Attributed to EUS guidance ability to visualize paragastric collateral circulation
RCT Comparing EUS-CYA + Coils vs EUS-CYA Alone
  • Patients with IGV1 and GOV2 varices, reassessed at 12 weeks, retreated if necessary
  • Outcomes (EUS-CYA + coils vs EUS-CYA alone):
  • Variceal obliteration: similar
  • Adverse events: similar
  • Reintervention rates: 20.8% vs 53.8% (P=.03) → favors coils
  • Time to reintervention: 44 weeks vs 25 weeks (P=.01) → favors coils
  • Survival: 48 weeks vs 42 weeks (P=.04) → favors coils
  • Glue volume: 1.5 cm³ vs 3.5 cm³ (P<.001) → favors coils
  • Patients received 1–4 coils per procedure
Cost Considerations
  • EUS-CYA + coils may be associated with less cost than EUS-CYA alone
  • Attributed to decreased needs for reintervention, hospitalizations, and lower glue volumes
Risk of Embolization
  • Low reported rates of pulmonary/systemic embolization after EUS-CYA (with/without coils)
  • Embolization can manifest as:
  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Coronary thromboembolism
  • Neurovascular thromboembolism
  • Asymptomatic ectopic pulmonary embolism also reported
Technical Tips for EUS-I Procedures
  • Risk of CYA polymerizing within working channel of EUS scope
  • CYA may occlude FNA needle or cause needle to stick within varix
  • Clinicians should familiarize themselves with techniques to avoid damage
Coil Selection and Deployment
  • Decision based on target vessel diameter and caliber of needle being used
  • 22-gauge needle requires 0.018-inch coil
  • 19-gauge needle compatible with both 0.018-inch and 0.035-inch coils
  • Deploy coils approximately 20%–30% greater in diameter than varix
CYA Formulations and Polymerization Rates
  • Available formulations: n-butyl-2-CYA and 2-octyl CYA
  • Slower polymerization agents (2-octyl CYA):
  • Lower risk of premature needle occlusion
  • ↑ concern for embolization → inject at slower rate, consider placement after coils
  • Faster polymerization agents (n-butyl-2-CYA):
  • Inject more rapidly to ↓ risk of premature needle occlusion
  • Rapid needle flush with sterile water or 5% dextrose in water after glue injection
  • Ethiodized oil (lipiodol) generally avoided due to embolization risk concerns
EUS-Guided Therapy vs Retrograde Transvenous Obliteration (RTO)
Initial Treatment of Gastric Varices
  • Best Practice Advice: ASGE suggests EUS-I be considered over RTO for initial management of high-risk gastric varices
  • Conditional recommendation / Very low certainty of evidence
Evidence for EUS-I vs RTO
  • Multicenter, propensity-matched analysis comparing EUS-I and RTO:
  • Included acute bleeding, primary prophylaxis, secondary prophylaxis
  • EUS-I included both EUS-CYA and EUS-CYA + coils
Outcomes (EUS-I vs RTO)
Outcome EUS-I RTO
Periprocedural adverse events 5.1% vs 22.0% (P=.007) —
Worsening of ascites 0% vs 15.3% (P=.003) —
Reintervention for gastric varices 28.8% vs 5.1% (P=.001) —
Unplanned intervention for worsening esophageal varices 1.7% vs 16.9% (P=.008) —
EUS-CYA + Coils vs Plug-Assisted RTO
  • Patients with EUS-CYA + coils vs plug-assisted RTO:
  • Less likely to develop ascites
  • More likely to require reintervention for gastric varices
  • Less likely to require reintervention for esophageal varices
Rationale for EUS-I Preference
  • RTO associated with ↑ adverse events (especially worsening ascites) relative to EUS-I
  • Performing EUS-I initially stabilizes patient → facilitates multidisciplinary discussions of best long-term management
Technical Expertise Considerations
  • Both RTO and EUS interventions are technically complex
  • Some concern that RTO may be more commonly available than EUS-I in some settings
  • Physicians should familiarize themselves with local expertise availability
TIPS and Radiologic Intervention After Endoscopic Therapy
Pre-emptive TIPS for Previously Treated Gastric Varices
  • Best Practice Advice: ASGE suggests multidisciplinary discussion to consider pre-emptive TIPS or other radiologic intervention
  • Conditional recommendation / Very low certainty of evidence
Evidence for Pre-emptive TIPS vs Continued Endoscopic Therapy
  • Multicenter RCT: patients with cirrhosis and gastric varices previously treated with DEI for active bleeding
  • Randomized to continued standard endoscopic glue therapy + NSBBs OR pre-emptive TIPS
Outcomes at 1 Year (Pre-emptive TIPS vs Standard Therapy)
Outcome Pre-emptive TIPS Standard Endoscopic Glue
Free from death or recurrent bleeding 77% vs 37% (P<.0001) —
  • Patients undergoing TIPS had similar rates of:
  • Jaundice
  • Ascites
  • Infection
  • Encephalopathy
  • Further decompensation
RCT Comparing Endoscopy vs Radiologic Intervention (BRTO/TIPS)
  • DEI for secondary prophylaxis of bleeding gastric varices
  • Radiologic intervention: BRTO when amenable shunt present; TIPS for those without
  • Exclusions: intractable ascites and portal vein thrombosis
Outcomes (Radiologic vs Endoscopy Alone)
Outcome Radiologic Intervention Endoscopy Alone
Gastric variceal recurrent bleeding 2.2% vs 24.4% (P=.04) —
Variceal bleeding–related mortality 2.2% vs 17.8% (P=.03) —
  • In radiologic arm, only single patient required additional CYA treatment
  • 26.7% of patients in CYA-only arm required 2 sessions of glue treatment
Adverse Events by Intervention Type
Outcome BRTO Group TIPS Group
Hepatic encephalopathy 6.7% vs 30% (P=.020) —
Ascites worsening 4.4% vs 36% (P=.001) —
  • Hepatic encephalopathy in TIPS group was medically manageable
  • Ascites in BRTO group was diuretic responsive
Patient-Specific Factors for Decision-Making
  • Consider: vascular anatomy (shunts, thrombosis), MELD-Na score, history of hepatic encephalopathy, intractable ascites
  • Patients with shunt-related hepatic encephalopathy → may benefit from RTO with shunt closure
  • Patients with poorly controlled ascites or large high-risk esophageal varices → may benefit from TIPS ± RTO
Note on Endoscopic Therapy Studies
  • In both trials, patients randomized to endoscopic therapy did not necessarily receive EUS-guided therapy with coils and CYA
  • Relevant because optimal EUS therapies may show less disparity between radiologic interventions and endoscopy
Summary of Changes from 2014 to Current Guidelines
Key Updates in ASGE Recommendations
Topic 2014 Guideline 2026 Guideline
Screening for varices in cACLD Endoscopy Baveno VI criteria
Management of cACLD and CSPH EVL or NSBB Carvedilol + endoscopy every 6–12 months
Length of vasoactive therapy 3–5 days 2–3 days
Timing of endoscopy Within 12 hours Within 24 hours
Management of aspiration risk PEI for all patients PEI not needed for all patients
Refractory variceal bleeding Balloon tamponade then TIPS Balloon tamponade or esophageal stent
Initial gastric variceal therapy Endoscopic CYA injection EUS-guided CYA and coils
Future Research Directions
  • Determine whether antibiotic prophylaxis is helpful for cirrhosis patients with upper GI bleeding
  • Better understand optimal timing of endoscopy in suspected variceal hemorrhage
  • Elicit optimal EUS therapy for gastric varices
  • Clarify optimal management of primary prophylaxis of gastric varices
  • Further refine risk stratification to avoid resource overutilization

Figure 2: Flowchart with suggestions for the management of patients with cirrhosis and high-risk gastric varices. *EUS-I methodologies include EUS injection of cyanoacrylate (CYA) or EUS injection of CYA with coils. Before therapy, stable patients without ongoing bleeding may have a 3-phase CT scan of the abdomen pelvis, a transdiaphragmatic echocardiogram with bubble agitation to assess for a patent foramen ovale, and a multidisciplinary discussion. In addition, if EUS-I expertise is not available, endoscopists can perform direct endoscopic injections for the management of gastric varices. BRTO, Balloon-assisted retrograde transvenous obliteration; EUS-I, endoscopic ultrasound-directed injection therapy; NSBB, nonselective beta-blocker; RTO, retrograde transvenous obliteration; TIPS, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt.
